problem: Two different things are collapsed into d. The first clause says d is the layer thickness removed in one pass (that is the uncut chip thickness t₁), and the second clause says the width of cut measured along the edge is taken as d in orthogonal tests. In the standard orthogonal model the width of cut is b (equal to the feed per revolution in tube turning, or to the plate width in planing/broaching); d is not the width along the edge. A student will write the wrong sentence in the exam.
fix: Depth of cut d (mm) is the thickness of the layer removed in one pass. In orthogonal tests d is the uncut chip thickness t₁; the width of cut b (mm), measured along the cutting edge, is the other dimension (b equals the feed in orthogonal tube turning).

where: Section 2, paragraph after the shear angle formula
problem: Internal contradiction. If r is held fixed, t₂ = t₁/r does not change, so the chip cannot be thinner. The last part of the sentence contradicts 'for the same r'.
fix: A larger rake angle α raises φ for the same r, so the shear plane becomes steeper. With t₁ fixed, a larger α raises r and the chip leaves thinner.

problem: Rake-angle names in oblique cutting are convention-dependent and the trap mixes them. The standard oblique model distinguishes the normal rake αn (measured in the plane normal to the cutting edge), the velocity rake and the effective rake αe (measured in the chip flow direction). In the usual tool-signature convention the side rake is measured in the plane normal to the side cutting edge, so calling it the opposite of the normal rake can mislead.
fix: In oblique cutting, state the rake you mean: the normal rake αn is measured in the normal plane, while the effective rake is measured in the chip flow direction. Do not mix the inclination angle i with the chip flow angle.
